specStatements.text: In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure, so diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
Students should be able to explain the properties of diamond in terms of its structure and bonding.
In graphite, each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers.
In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
Students should be able to explain the properties of graphite in terms of its structure and bonding.
Students should know that graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.
Graphene is a single layer of graphite and has properties that make it useful in electronics and composites.
Students should be able to explain the properties of graphene in terms of its structure and bonding.

Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms. The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀ ) which has a spherical shape.
Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios. Their properties make them useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.
recognise graphene and fullerenes from diagrams and descriptions of their bonding and structure
give examples of the uses of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes.

scopeNotes.statement: In diamond, each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure, so diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Diamond is treated at exactly the depth the specification states: four covalent bonds per carbon atom, a giant covalent structure, and the three named consequences (very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct electricity). No item asks for bond angles, for the tetrahedral geometry by name, for hybridisation, for lattice energies or for numerical melting points, and no item requires diamond to be compared with silicon dioxide, because none of that appears in this section.

scopeNotes.statement: In graphite, each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification says only that there are no covalent bonds between the layers. Items therefore test the absence of covalent bonding between layers and never require the attraction between layers to be named, quantified or classified as a particular type of intermolecular force. Where a distractor mentions such forces it is marked wrong for the reason the specification gives, not for the name it uses.

scopeNotes.statement: Graphene is a single layer of graphite and has properties that make it useful in electronics and composites.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Graphene is taught only as what the specification calls it - a single layer of graphite - and its usefulness is explained from that structure alone: strong covalent bonds within the sheet and one delocalised electron per carbon atom. The two application areas named, electronics and composites, are the only ones used. Nothing is asked about how graphene is made, about measured values of its strength or conductivity, or about electronic band theory.

scopeNotes.statement: Carbon nanotubes are cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios. Their properties make them useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Nanotubes are treated as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios, useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials. No item asks for methods of synthesis, for single-walled versus multi-walled distinctions, for chirality, or for numerical values of tensile strength or conductivity, none of which the specification requires.

concepts.definition: A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms in a giant covalent structure. Diamond is very hard, has a very high melting point and does not conduct electricity.
A structure in which very many atoms are joined to one another by covalent bonds in a continuous network, so that there are no separate molecules. Diamond and graphite are giant covalent structures.
A shared pair of electrons between two atoms. Covalent bonds are strong, so a great deal of energy is needed to break the many covalent bonds in a giant covalent structure.
A form of carbon in which each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms, forming layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers.
A ring of six carbon atoms. The layers in graphite, and the sheet in graphene, are built from hexagonal rings of carbon atoms.
An electron that is not held in a bond between two particular atoms and is free to move through the structure. In graphite, one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
A single layer of graphite. Its properties make it useful in electronics and composites.
A molecule of carbon atoms with a hollow shape. The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
The first fullerene to be discovered, C₆₀, which has a spherical shape.
A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio. Carbon nanotubes are useful for nanotechnology, electronics and materials.
How many times longer a shape is than it is wide. Carbon nanotubes have very high length to diameter ratios: they are extremely long compared with how narrow they are.
A material made by combining two materials so that the mixture has properties neither has alone. Graphene and carbon nanotubes are added to composites to strengthen them.

misconceptions.question: Why is graphite soft enough to write with?
misconceptions.correct: Graphite gives way between its layers, where there are no covalent bonds at all, so whole layers slide over one another. The covalent bonds inside each layer are strong and are not broken.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphite is soft because the covalent bonds in graphite are weak.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link 'soft' straight to 'weak bonds'. Because graphite rubs off onto paper they assume whatever holds it together must be feeble, and they never separate the bonding inside a layer from what is between the layers.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the sliding happens. It happens between the layers, where the specification says there are no covalent bonds. Inside each layer the covalent bonds are strong, which is why graphite still has a very high melting point.

misconceptions.question: What has to be broken to melt diamond?
misconceptions.correct: Many strong covalent bonds have to be broken, because diamond is a giant covalent structure with no separate molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Diamond is made of small carbon molecules held together by weak forces, so melting it only separates the molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet covalent bonding first in small molecules such as CO₂ and carry the 'covalent means molecular, so weak forces between molecules' rule straight over to diamond.
misconceptions.correction: Point out that no molecule can be found in diamond: the covalent bonds run right through the whole crystal. There is nothing between molecules to overcome, so the covalent bonds themselves must be broken.

misconceptions.question: Does diamond conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Diamond does not conduct electricity, because all four outer electrons of every carbon atom are used in covalent bonds and none is delocalised.
misconceptions.misconception: The different forms of carbon are interchangeable, so diamond and graphite have the same structure and properties (for example, each conducts electricity).
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diamond and graphite are taught together as forms of carbon, so students generalise the property of one to the other, sometimes helped by knowing that diamond does conduct heat well.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the bonding, not the element. Graphite conducts because each carbon uses only three of its outer electrons in bonds, leaving one delocalised. Diamond uses all four, so it has no delocalised electrons.

misconceptions.question: Where are diamond's delocalised electrons?
misconceptions.correct: Diamond has no delocalised electrons at all. Every outer electron of every carbon atom is in a covalent bond.
misconceptions.misconception: Diamond has delocalised electrons, but they are trapped and cannot move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember 'no conduction' and invent a reason that keeps the electrons: they picture delocalised electrons that are somehow stuck, rather than accepting that there are none.
misconceptions.correction: Count the electrons. Carbon has four outer electrons and forms four bonds in diamond, so four out of four are used. Nothing is left over to be delocalised.

misconceptions.question: How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form in graphite?
misconceptions.correct: Three. Each carbon atom forms three covalent bonds with three other carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Each carbon atom in graphite forms four covalent bonds, because carbon always forms four.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Carbon always makes four bonds' is a rule students learn early and apply everywhere. Graphite is the exception they must hold in mind alongside it.
misconceptions.correction: Tie the number of bonds to the delocalised electron. Carbon still has four outer electrons in graphite, but only three go into bonds; the fourth is the one that is delocalised.

misconceptions.question: What is between the layers in graphite?
misconceptions.correct: There are no covalent bonds between the layers of graphite.
misconceptions.misconception: In both diamond and graphite the atoms lie in layers, and adjacent layers are joined to one another by covalent bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams of graphite draw dotted or faint lines between the layers to show the stacking, and students read those lines as bonds.
misconceptions.correction: Read the specification wording: layers of hexagonal rings which have no covalent bonds between the layers. If covalent bonds joined the layers, the layers could not slide and graphite could not mark paper.

misconceptions.question: How many electrons from each carbon atom in graphite are delocalised?
misconceptions.correct: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.
misconceptions.misconception: All four outer electrons from each carbon atom in graphite are delocalised.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer the metal picture wholesale - positive ions in a sea of electrons - and assume every outer electron joins the sea.
misconceptions.correction: Only the electron left over after the three covalent bonds is delocalised, so it is one per carbon atom. Three of the four outer electrons are still held in bonds.

misconceptions.question: Does graphite have a high or a low melting point?
misconceptions.correct: Graphite has a very high melting point, because melting it means breaking the many strong covalent bonds within its layers.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphite has a low melting point because its layers slide over one another so easily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students merge two separate properties: sliding layers make graphite soft, and softness feels like something that would melt easily.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two questions. Sliding needs nothing to be broken, so graphite is soft. Melting needs the strong covalent bonds inside the layers to be broken, so the melting point is very high.

misconceptions.question: Is graphene a hollow cage of carbon atoms?
misconceptions.correct: No. Graphene is a single layer of graphite: one flat sheet of carbon atoms joined in hexagonal rings.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphene is a hollow ball or cage of carbon atoms, like Buckminsterfullerene.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Graphene, fullerenes and nanotubes are met in the same lesson as 'the new carbon structures', and the striking football image of C₆₀ attaches itself to whichever name is being asked about.
misconceptions.correction: Anchor graphene to graphite, not to fullerenes. Peel one layer off graphite and you have graphene - it is flat and open, not closed into a cage.

misconceptions.question: How thick is graphene?
misconceptions.correct: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, so it is one atom thick.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphene is a thin stack of several graphite layers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Thin' is easier to hold on to than 'single layer', so students settle for a few layers rather than exactly one.
misconceptions.correction: The specification defines graphene as a single layer of graphite. One layer, not a few; that is the whole definition.

misconceptions.question: Are fullerenes giant covalent structures?
misconceptions.correct: No. Fullerenes are molecules of carbon atoms with hollow shapes, so each fullerene is a separate molecule with a definite formula, such as C₆₀.
misconceptions.misconception: Fullerenes are giant covalent structures like diamond and graphite.
misconceptions.whyItArises: All the other forms of carbon in this topic are giant structures, so students expect fullerenes to be giant too, and the word 'carbon' triggers the giant covalent answer automatically.
misconceptions.correction: A giant structure is a continuous network with no separate molecules, so its formula only gives the ratio of atoms - carbon itself is written C. A fullerene is a separate molecule, and C₆₀ counts the atoms in one of them. That is why fullerenes have hollow shapes and definite sizes.

misconceptions.question: Which rings are found in fullerenes?
misconceptions.correct: The structure of fullerenes is based on hexagonal rings of carbon atoms, but they may also contain rings with five or seven carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Fullerenes are built only from hexagonal rings, exactly like graphite layers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Fullerene structures are introduced straight after graphite, and the hexagon is the shape students have just been drilled on, so the five- and seven-membered rings are dropped.
misconceptions.correction: A sheet of hexagons alone stays flat. The rings of five, and sometimes seven, are what let the sheet curve round and close into a hollow shape.

misconceptions.question: What shape is a carbon nanotube?
misconceptions.correct: A carbon nanotube is a cylindrical fullerene, so it is a hollow tube, with a very high length to diameter ratio.
misconceptions.misconception: A carbon nanotube is a solid rod of carbon, like a very thin piece of pencil lead.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'tube' is read as 'rod' or 'wire' once students picture nanotubes reinforcing materials or carrying current, and the fullerene link is forgotten.
misconceptions.correction: The specification calls nanotubes cylindrical fullerenes, and every fullerene is hollow. The carbon atoms lie in the wall of the tube; the inside is empty.

misconceptions.question: What is diamond made of?
misconceptions.correct: Diamond is made of carbon atoms only, each one forming four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: Diamond must contain some other element as well, or it could not be so much harder than graphite.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that two substances with such different properties cannot be made of the same thing, so they assume something extra must have been added to diamond.
misconceptions.correction: Both are carbon; only the bonding differs. Four bonds per atom in three dimensions gives diamond, three bonds per atom in layers gives graphite.

misconceptions.question: What carries the current when a solid conducts electricity?
misconceptions.correct: In graphite and in metals the current is carried by delocalised electrons moving through the structure.
misconceptions.misconception: Only ions that are free to move can carry an electric current, so a solid without ions cannot conduct.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule 'ions must be free to move' is learned for molten and dissolved ionic compounds and is then applied to every conducting substance.
misconceptions.correction: Ions are not the only charge carriers. Graphite contains no ions at all, yet it conducts, because one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and free to move.

misconceptions.question: In what way is graphite like a metal?
misconceptions.correct: Graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Graphite is like a metal because it is made of positive ions held in a sea of electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students take the whole metallic bonding model across at once instead of the single feature the specification names.
misconceptions.correction: The similarity the specification asks for is the delocalised electrons, and that is all. Graphite is built from carbon atoms held by covalent bonds, not from positive ions.

mcqs.stem: In diamond, how many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and with what?

options.text: Four covalent bonds, with four other carbon atoms
options.rationale: The specification states that in diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds with other carbon atoms.

options.text: Four covalent bonds, to atoms of other elements
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume something other than carbon must be present to make diamond so hard.

options.text: Four covalent bonds, inside a small molecule
options.rationale: Students who treat every covalent substance as molecular get the number right but picture separate molecules.

options.text: Three covalent bonds, to other carbon atoms
options.rationale: This is graphite's figure, recalled for the wrong form of carbon because the two are learned together.

mcqs.stem: Which set of properties does diamond have?

options.text: Very hard, low melting point, does not conduct
options.rationale: Keeps the hardness but treats diamond as though only weak forces between molecules had to be overcome.

options.text: Very hard, very high melting point, does not conduct
options.rationale: These are exactly the three properties of diamond given by the specification.

options.text: Very hard, very high melting point, conducts electricity
options.rationale: Chosen by students who assume that any form of carbon conducts electricity because graphite does.

options.text: Soft and slippery, high melting point, conducts
options.rationale: This is the graphite property set, attached to diamond by students who mix the two forms up.

mcqs.stem: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.

options.text: The weak forces between diamond's molecules must be overcome
options.rationale: The standard simple-molecular explanation, applied to a substance that contains no molecules at all.

options.text: The delocalised electrons hold the carbon atoms in place
options.rationale: Invents delocalised electrons in diamond, where all four outer electrons are held in covalent bonds.

options.text: Many strong covalent bonds have to be broken to melt it
options.rationale: Diamond is a giant covalent structure, so melting it means breaking very many strong covalent bonds.

options.text: Its carbon molecules are heavy, so more energy is used
options.rationale: Uses the 'bigger molecules melt higher' rule on a giant structure that has no molecules to separate.

mcqs.stem: Explain why diamond does not conduct electricity.

options.text: Covalent bonds between its layers stop electrons moving
options.rationale: Gives diamond layers, which belong to graphite, and misplaces where the covalent bonds are.

options.text: Its delocalised electrons cannot move through the structure
options.rationale: Keeps the delocalised electrons and makes them stuck, rather than accepting that there are none.

options.text: It has no ions, and only ions can carry a current in a solid
options.rationale: Applies the rule for molten ionic compounds; it would wrongly rule out graphite and metals too.

options.text: All four outer electrons of each carbon are in bonds
options.rationale: With every outer electron used in a covalent bond, diamond has no delocalised electrons to carry charge.

mcqs.stem: In graphite, how many other carbon atoms is each carbon atom bonded to, and how are the atoms arranged?

options.text: Four others, in layers built from rings of six atoms
options.rationale: Gets the layers right but keeps the 'carbon always forms four bonds' rule.

options.text: Three others, in layers built from rings of six carbon atoms
options.rationale: The specification states three covalent bonds per carbon atom, forming layers of hexagonal rings.

options.text: Three others, in a giant three-dimensional network
options.rationale: Gets the number of bonds right but gives diamond's arrangement instead of layers.

options.text: Three others, in rings of five joined into a hollow ball
options.rationale: Confuses graphite with a fullerene cage, which is closed rather than made of flat layers.

mcqs.stem: What does the specification say about bonding between the layers in graphite?

options.text: Strong covalent bonds join each layer to the next
options.rationale: Reads the faint stacking lines on a graphite diagram as though they were bonds.

options.text: The delocalised electrons form covalent bonds between layers
options.rationale: Turns the delocalised electrons into bonds, which would stop the layers sliding.

options.text: There are no covalent bonds between graphite's layers
options.rationale: The specification says the layers of hexagonal rings have no covalent bonds between the layers.

options.text: Each layer shares pairs of electrons with the next
options.rationale: Another wording of covalent bonding between layers, chosen for the same reason.

mcqs.stem: How many electrons from each carbon atom in graphite are delocalised?

options.text: All four of the outer electrons of every carbon atom
options.rationale: Transfers the metallic 'sea of electrons' picture and delocalises every outer electron.

options.text: Two electrons from each atom, leaving 2+ ions in the sea
options.rationale: A halfway answer from students who know some electrons are left over but not how many.

options.text: None: every electron in graphite is in a bond
options.rationale: Would leave graphite unable to conduct, contradicting a property students already know.

options.text: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised
options.rationale: The specification states that in graphite one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised.

mcqs.stem: Explain why graphite is soft enough to leave a mark on paper.

options.text: Layers slide off because no covalent bonds join them
options.rationale: With no covalent bonds between the layers, whole layers slide over one another and rub off.

options.text: Its covalent bonds are weak, so the structure crumbles
options.rationale: The classic soft-means-weak error; the covalent bonds within each layer are strong.

options.text: Its delocalised electrons let the carbon atoms slide past
options.rationale: Gives the delocalised electrons a mechanical job that they do not do.

options.text: Graphite melts at a low temperature and rubs away easily
options.rationale: Muddles softness with melting point; graphite's melting point is in fact very high.

options.text: Its carbon atoms move along the layers carrying charge
options.rationale: Confuses moving atoms with moving electrons; the carbon atoms stay bonded in place.

options.text: Ions in graphite are free to move between the layers
options.rationale: Applies the ionic rule; graphite contains no ions, only carbon atoms and electrons.

options.text: One delocalised electron per carbon atom can move through it
options.rationale: One electron from each carbon atom is delocalised, and delocalised electrons are free to move.

options.text: Each carbon has a spare electron held in a covalent bond
options.rationale: Half remembers the spare electron but leaves it in a bond, where it could not carry charge.

mcqs.stem: In what way is graphite similar to a metal?

options.text: It can be hammered into new shapes without breaking
options.rationale: Borrows malleability, a metallic property the specification does not give graphite.

options.text: It is held together by strong ionic bonds, as metals are
options.rationale: Gets metallic bonding wrong as well; neither graphite nor a metal is held by ionic bonds.

options.text: It is built from positive ions in a sea of electrons
options.rationale: Takes the whole metallic model across instead of the one feature the specification names.

options.text: It contains delocalised electrons that are free to move
options.rationale: The specification says graphite is similar to metals in that it has delocalised electrons.

options.text: A single layer of graphite, exactly one atom thick
options.rationale: The specification defines graphene as a single layer of graphite.

options.text: A stack of several graphite layers bonded firmly together
options.rationale: Settles for 'thin' rather than the single layer the specification requires.

options.text: A hollow ball of carbon atoms, like Buckminsterfullerene
options.rationale: Attaches the striking C60 football image to the wrong name.

options.text: A giant carbon structure with four bonds per atom
options.rationale: Describes diamond's bonding, using the 'carbon always forms four bonds' rule.

mcqs.stem: Graphene is useful in electronics. Which explanation of this uses graphene's structure and bonding correctly?

options.text: It conducts, because its weak covalent bonds free the electrons
options.rationale: Weak covalent bonds (m01) are wrongly thought to release electrons that carry the current.

options.text: It conducts: each carbon has a delocalised electron
options.rationale: Graphene is a single layer of graphite, so one electron from each carbon atom is delocalised and free to move.

options.text: It does not conduct: all four outer electrons are in bonds
options.rationale: Applies diamond's bonding to graphene, which would make it useless in electronics.

options.text: It conducts, because it is a hollow cage that traps ions
options.rationale: Treats graphene as a fullerene and brings in ions that are not there.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about Buckminsterfullerene is correct?

options.text: It is a giant covalent structure with the formula C₆₀
options.rationale: Keeps the giant structure habit from diamond and graphite, though C60 is a molecule.

options.text: It is a solid ball of carbon, with the formula C₆₀
options.rationale: Thinks fullerenes are solid, not hollow (m13), so pictures C60 as a solid ball.

options.text: It is a flat sheet of carbon with the formula C₆₀
options.rationale: Gives C60 graphene's flat shape, losing the hollow cage the specification describes.

options.text: It is a hollow, spherical molecule with the formula C₆₀
options.rationale: The first fullerene to be discovered was Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀ ), which has a spherical shape.

mcqs.stem: A structure is described as a hollow cage of carbon atoms built from hexagonal rings together with some rings of five carbon atoms. What is it?

options.text: A fullerene, as its cage can contain rings of five atoms
options.rationale: Fullerenes are hollow molecules based on hexagonal rings that may also contain rings of five or seven carbon atoms.

options.text: Graphene, because a graphene sheet is a hollow carbon cage
options.rationale: The commonest graphene error: a single flat layer is described as a cage.

options.text: Diamond, because its rings can hold five carbon atoms
options.rationale: Reaches for the most familiar form of carbon without checking the hollow cage.

options.text: Graphite, because its layers curl into hollow cages
options.rationale: Keeps hexagons only, and imagines a flat layer closing up without any rings of five.

mcqs.stem: Which description fits a carbon nanotube?

options.text: A solid rod of pure carbon with a very high length to diameter ratio
options.rationale: Reads 'tube' as 'rod'; every fullerene, including a nanotube, is hollow.

options.text: A cylindrical fullerene with a very high length to diameter ratio
options.rationale: The specification describes carbon nanotubes as cylindrical fullerenes with very high length to diameter ratios.

options.text: A sphere of carbon atoms with a very high length to diameter ratio
options.rationale: Uses the C60 shape; a sphere cannot have a high length to diameter ratio.

options.text: A tube of diamond with a very high length to diameter ratio
options.rationale: Reaches for diamond because nanotubes are also described as strong.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a use of fullerenes, including carbon nanotubes?

options.text: Cutting and drilling hard rock, as they are the hardest
options.rationale: A use of diamond, chosen because nanotubes are also described as strong.

options.text: Lining furnaces, as they melt at a very high temperature
options.rationale: Treats fullerenes as giant covalent structures with very high melting points.

options.text: Strengthening composites and use in electronics
options.rationale: The specification names nanotechnology, electronics and materials as uses of carbon nanotubes.

options.text: Making pencil leads slide smoothly across the paper
options.rationale: A use of graphite, which depends on layers sliding, not on hollow carbon molecules.
